question: Which statement best describes Minimize client JavaScript (Server Components)?
options: The biggest perf lever in the App Router is keeping components on the server. Server Components render to HTML on the server and ship ZERO JavaScript for that component, so only the genuinely interactive 'use client' islands cost bundle and hydration time. Pushing data fetching and static markup to Server Components, and keeping client islands small and leaf-level, directly improves load and interactivity.

next/dynamic lazy-loads a Client Component so its JS isn't in the initial bundle — it downloads only when rendered. This is ideal for heavy, below-the-fold, or modal-only widgets (charts, editors, maps). You can pass a loading fallback and `ssr: false` to skip server rendering for browser-only libs.

next/image automatically serves correctly-sized, modern-format (AVIF/WebP), lazy-loaded images and reserves space to avoid layout shift; setting `priority` on the LCP image speeds first paint. next/font self-hosts fonts at build time, removing render-blocking requests and preventing font-related CLS. Together they target LCP and CLS directly.

Serving pages/data from cache (static rendering, ISR, the Data Cache, and the Full Route Cache) means most requests hit a CDN or memoized result instead of doing per-request work — drastically lowering TTFB. ISR keeps content static-fast while refreshing on a revalidate interval; revalidateTag/Path give targeted freshness without global no-store.

question: Which statement best describes Code splitting & dynamic import (next/dynamic)?
options: With Suspense and loading.tsx, Next streams HTML in chunks: the static shell and fast parts paint immediately while slow data 'holes' stream in as they resolve. This improves perceived speed and TTFB because the user isn't blocked on the slowest query, and it's the basis of Partial Prerendering.

question: Which statement best describes Image & font optimization?
options: LCP measures when the largest content paints (target < 2.5s), CLS measures unexpected layout shift (target < 0.1), and INP measures responsiveness to interactions (target < 200ms). Server rendering + image priority improve LCP, reserving space + next/font improve CLS, and smaller client JS improves INP. These are Google ranking signals.

@next/bundle-analyzer (or the build's bundle report) visualizes what's in each route's JavaScript. It exposes accidental heavy client dependencies, duplicated libraries, and components that shouldn't be client. Acting on it — dynamic-importing, moving code to the server, swapping heavy libs — is how you keep INP and load time low.

next/link automatically prefetches the JS and (in the App Router) cached RSC payload for in-viewport links, so navigating feels instant.
